subproblem.title: The segment-averaged right-hand side is a Hoelder family of linear forms on L(R^n, R^l)
subproblem.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, alpha > 0, H and d real numbers, g : R^n -> R^l, S and K subsets of R^n and e in R^n, such that x + (td)e lies in K for all x in S and t in [0,1], and ||g(x) - g(y)|| <= H ||x - y||^alpha for x, y in K. Then there is a map Phi from R^n to continuous linear forms on L := L(R^n, R^l) such that Phi(x)[P] = < integral_0^1 g(x + (td)e) dt , Pe > for all x in R^n and P in L, and |Phi(x)[P] - Phi(y)[P]| <= H ||e|| ||x - y||^alpha ||P|| for all x, y in S and P in L.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (α H d : ℝ) (g : Rn n → Rn ℓ) (S K : Set (Rn n)) (e : Rn n), 0 < α → (∀ x ∈ S, ∀ t ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, x + (t * d) • e ∈ K) → (∀ x ∈ K, ∀ y ∈ K, ‖g x - g y‖ ≤ H * ‖x - y‖ ^ α) → ∃ Φ : Rn n → (Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ) →L[ℝ] ℝ, (∀ (x : Rn n) (P : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ), Φ x P = inner ℝ (∫ t in (0 : ℝ)..1, g (x + (t * d) • e)) (P e)) ∧ ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ y ∈ S, ∀ P : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, |Φ x P - Φ y P| ≤ H * ‖e‖ * ‖x - y‖ ^ α * ‖P‖
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 4 (definition of the forcing Phi_d) and Step 5 (H4) of the parent proof.
1. Definition. G(x) := integral_0^1 g(x + (td)e) dt in R^l (an interval integral, defined for every x). Phi(x) is the composition of the continuous linear map P -> Pe (evaluation at e, L -> R^l; ContinuousLinearMap.apply) with the continuous linear form v -> <G(x), v> (innerSL). So Phi(x) is a continuous linear form on L and Phi(x)[P] = <G(x), Pe> for all x and P.
2. g is continuous on K: for p, q in K, ||g(q) - g(p)|| <= H||q - p||^alpha <= max(H, 0)||q - p||^alpha, and max(H, 0)||q - p||^alpha -> 0 as q -> p because alpha > 0 (continuity of r -> r^alpha at 0, where it vanishes).
3. For x in S, t -> x + (td)e is continuous and maps [0,1] into K, so t -> g(x + (td)e) is continuous on [0,1] and therefore interval integrable on [0,1].
4. For x, y in S and t in [0,1], both x + (td)e and y + (td)e lie in K and their difference is x - y, so ||g(x + (td)e) - g(y + (td)e)|| <= H||x - y||^alpha. By step 3, G(x) - G(y) = integral_0^1 (g(x + (td)e) - g(y + (td)e)) dt (intervalIntegral.integral_sub), and the constant bound on (0,1] gives ||G(x) - G(y)|| <= H||x - y||^alpha |1 - 0| = H||x - y||^alpha (intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const).
5. For x, y in S and P in L: Phi(x)[P] - Phi(y)[P] = <G(x) - G(y), Pe> (inner_sub_left). By Cauchy-Schwarz and ||Pe|| <= ||P|| ||e||, |Phi(x)[P] - Phi(y)[P]| <= ||G(x) - G(y)|| ||P|| ||e|| <= H||x - y||^alpha ||P|| ||e|| = H||e|| ||x - y||^alpha ||P||, multiplying the inequality of step 4 by ||P|| ||e|| >= 0. QED

Then (i) w is C^1 on V; (ii) Dw(x) = d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x)) for x in V; (iii) ||w(x)|| <= eps ||e|| for x in V; (iv) ||Dw(x) - Dw(y)|| <= 2 |d|^{-1} H ||x - y||^alpha for x, y in V.

Source: Step 3 and Step 5 (H5)-(H7) of the parent proof.
1. For x in V the whole segment {x + (td)e : t in [0,1]} lies in K, a subset of U; in particular x (t = 0) and x + de (t = 1) lie in K. Since U is open and u is C^1 on U, u is differentiable at every point of U.
2. (i) The translation z -> z + de is smooth and maps V into U (step 1), so z -> u(z + de) is C^1 on V (ContDiffOn.comp); u is C^1 on V, a subset of U (ContDiffOn.mono). Hence w = d^{-1}(u(. + de) - u) is C^1 on V.
3. (ii) Fix x in V. u is differentiable at x + de, so z -> u(z + de) has derivative Du(x + de) at x (chain rule with the translation); u has derivative Du(x) at x. By linearity of the derivative, w has derivative d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x)) at x, so Dw(x) = d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x)).
4. (iii) Fix x in V and let h(t) := u(x + (td)e). For t in [0,1], x + (td)e lies in K, a subset of U, so h has derivative h'(t) = Du(x + (td)e)[de] with ||h'(t)|| <= ||Du(x + (td)e)|| ||de|| <= eps |d| ||e|| (multiplying ||Du|| <= eps by ||de|| >= 0). By the mean value inequality on [0,1] (norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_deriv_le_segment_01'), ||u(x + de) - u(x)|| = ||h(1) - h(0)|| <= eps |d| ||e||. Hence ||w(x)|| = |d|^{-1} ||u(x + de) - u(x)|| <= |d|^{-1} eps |d| ||e|| = eps ||e|| (d nonzero).
5. (iv) For x, y in V, by (ii): Dw(x) - Dw(y) = d^{-1}[(Du(x + de) - Du(y + de)) - (Du(x) - Du(y))]. The four points x, y, x + de, y + de lie in K (step 1) and (x + de) - (y + de) = x - y, so ||Dw(x) - Dw(y)|| <= |d|^{-1}(H||x - y||^alpha + H||x - y||^alpha) = 2|d|^{-1} H ||x - y||^alpha. QED

Source: Step 1 of the parent proof (the constants M_B, L_B of Psi on the closed eps-ball), written out in full.
Notation. L is a finite-dimensional real normed space, so its closed balls are compact. Let L* := L(L, R) and Bil := L(L, L*) be the spaces of continuous linear forms and of continuous bilinear forms on L with their operator norms; for beta in Bil and Q, Q' in L, |beta[Q][Q']| <= ||beta[Q]|| ||Q'|| <= ||beta|| ||Q|| ||Q'|| (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm2). Put A := D Psi : L -> L* and B := D A : L -> Bil, so that B(P)[Q][Q'] = fderiv R (fderiv R Psi) P Q Q'.
1. Regularity. Psi is C^3, hence A = fderiv R Psi is C^2 and B = fderiv R A is C^1 (ContDiff.fderiv_right, twice). So B is continuous, B is differentiable at every point, and its derivative DB = fderiv R B : L -> L(L, Bil) is continuous (ContDiff.continuous_fderiv).
2. The set Kc := closedBall(0, eps) in L is compact (finite dimension; for eps < 0 it is empty, which is also compact) and convex.
3. Bound (i). B is continuous on the compact set Kc, so there is M with ||B(P)|| <= M for all P in Kc (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn). Put M_B := max(M, 0) >= 0. For P with ||P|| <= eps (that is, P in Kc) and any Q, Q' in L: |B(P)[Q][Q']| <= ||B(P)|| ||Q|| ||Q'|| <= M_B ||Q|| ||Q'||, using ||Q|| ||Q'|| >= 0.
4. Lipschitz estimate for B. DB is continuous on Kc, so there is L0 with ||DB(P)|| <= L0 for P in Kc; put L_B := max(L0, 0) >= 0. Kc is convex, B is differentiable at every point of Kc and ||DB|| <= L_B on Kc, so the mean value inequality on convex sets (Convex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_fderiv_le) gives ||B(P) - B(P')|| <= L_B ||P - P'|| for all P, P' in Kc.
5. Bound (ii). For P, P' in Kc and Q, Q' in L, B(P)[Q][Q'] - B(P')[Q][Q'] = (B(P) - B(P'))[Q][Q'], so by the Notation paragraph and step 4, |B(P)[Q][Q'] - B(P')[Q][Q']| <= ||B(P) - B(P')|| ||Q|| ||Q'|| <= L_B ||P - P'|| ||Q|| ||Q'||. Steps 3 and 5 prove the claim with M_B, L_B >= 0. QED

subproblem.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, U an open subset of R^n, g : R^n -> R^l continuous on U, zeta : R^n -> R^l of class C^1 with compact support, e in R^n and d in R, such that x + (td)e lies in U for every x in tsupport zeta and every t in [0,1]. Then the integral over R^n of <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx equals d times the integral over R^n of < integral_0^1 g(x + (td)e) dt , Dzeta(x)e > dx.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 4(c) of the parent proof (the computation of the right-hand side of the difference-quotient equation), isolated as an identity about zeta and g only.
Notation. K := tsupport zeta (compact and closed). K' := {y + (sd)e : y in K, s in [0,1]} is compact (continuous image of [0,1] x K) and contained in U by hypothesis. Lebesgue measure on R^n is translation invariant: integral F(y + c) dy = integral F(y) dy for every F and every c (integral_add_right_eq_self; no integrability is needed). zeta and Dzeta are continuous, zeta(y) = 0 and Dzeta(y) = 0 for y not in K (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), and g is continuous at every point of U (U is open). Let c(s) := max(0, min(s, 1)) be the clamp of s to [0,1]: c is continuous, c(s) lies in [0,1], and c(s) = s for s in [0,1]. Write G(y) := integral_0^1 g(y + (td)e) dt.
1. Difference formula. Fix x. k(s) := zeta(x - (sd)e) has derivative k'(s) = Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[-(de)] = -d Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] (chain rule), continuous in s. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt), zeta(x - de) - zeta(x) = k(1) - k(0) = -d integral_0^1 Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] ds, i.e. zeta(x) - zeta(x - de) = d integral_0^1 Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] ds.
2. Put F(s, x) := <Dzeta(x - (c(s)d)e)[e], g(x)>. By step 1, <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> = d * integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds for every x: pull d out of the inner product; on [0,1] one has c(s) = s (intervalIntegral.integral_congr); the continuous linear form v -> <g(x), v> commutes with the interval integral of the continuous integrand (ContinuousLinearMap.intervalIntegral_comp_comm with innerSL); the real inner product is symmetric.
3. F is continuous on R x R^n. Let (s, x) be given. If x - (c(s)d)e is not in K, then, K being closed and (s', x') -> x' - (c(s')d)e continuous, Dzeta vanishes at x' - (c(s')d)e for (s', x') near (s, x), so F = 0 near (s, x). If x - (c(s)d)e is in K, then x = (x - (c(s)d)e) + (c(s)d)e lies in U (hypothesis with t = c(s)), so g is continuous at x and F, an inner product of functions continuous at (s, x), is continuous at (s, x).
4. Integrability of F. F(s, x) = 0 whenever x is not in K' (if x - (c(s)d)e were in K, x would lie in K'). F is continuous, so it is integrable on the compact set [0,1] x K' for the product of Lebesgue measures (ContinuousOn.integrableOn_compact), hence on [0,1] x R^n since it vanishes on the rest (IntegrableOn.of_forall_sdiff_eq_zero), hence on (0,1] x R^n. Since (Lebesgue restricted to (0,1]) x Lebesgue = (Lebesgue x Lebesgue) restricted to (0,1] x R^n (Measure.prod_restrict), F is integrable for the measure used by Fubini's theorem for interval integrals.
5. Let Ft(s, y) := <Dzeta(y)[e], g(y + (c(s)d)e)>. If y is not in K, Ft vanishes near (s, y) (K closed); if y is in K, y + (c(s)d)e lies in U and g is continuous there. So Ft is continuous, vanishes outside R x K, and exactly as in step 4 it is integrable on (0,1] x R^n.
6. Translation. For each s, by translation invariance with x = y + (c(s)d)e: integral F(s, x) dx = integral F(s, y + (c(s)d)e) dy = integral Ft(s, y) dy.
7. Inner integral of Ft. For y in K the map s -> g(y + (sd)e) is continuous on [0,1] (the segment lies in U), hence interval integrable, and integral_0^1 Ft(s, y) ds = integral_0^1 <Dzeta(y)[e], g(y + (sd)e)> ds = <Dzeta(y)[e], G(y)> = <G(y), Dzeta(y)e> (c(s) = s on [0,1]; innerSL commutes with the integral; symmetry). For y not in K both sides are 0 because Dzeta(y) = 0.
8. Chain. integral <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx = integral d * (integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds) dx [step 2] = d * integral (integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds) dx [integral_const_mul] = d * integral_0^1 (integral F(s, x) dx) ds [Fubini, intervalIntegral_integral_swap with step 4] = d * integral_0^1 (integral Ft(s, y) dy) ds [step 6] = d * integral (integral_0^1 Ft(s, y) ds) dy [Fubini with step 5] = d * integral <G(y), Dzeta(y)e> dy [step 7]. QED

subproblem.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, L := L(R^n, R^l), Psi : L -> R of class C^2 with A := D Psi and B := D^2 Psi, U and V open subsets of R^n, u, g : R^n -> R^l with u of class C^1 on U and g continuous on U, e in R^n and d a nonzero real number, such that x + (td)e lies in U for all x in V and t in [0,1]. Assume that the integral over U of A(Du(x))[Dphi(x)] dx equals minus the integral over U of <phi(x), g(x)> dx for every C^1 compactly supported phi : R^n -> R^l with tsupport phi contained in U. Then for every C^1 compactly supported zeta : R^n -> R^l with tsupport zeta contained in V: the integral over V of ( integral_0^1 B(Du(x) + t(Du(x + de) - Du(x)))[d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x))][Dzeta(x)] dt ) dx equals the integral over V of < integral_0^1 g(x + (td)e) dt , Dzeta(x)e > dx.

Source: Step 4(a), (b) and (d) of the parent proof; the right-hand side computation 4(c) is the sibling dohr_eb_elc2_shift_ibp.
Notation. Delta(y) := Du(y + de) - Du(y), P_t(y) := Du(y) + t Delta(y), I(y) := integral_0^1 B(P_t(y))[d^{-1}Delta(y)][Dzeta(y)] dt, G(y) := integral_0^1 g(y + (td)e) dt and J(y) := <G(y), Dzeta(y)e>. The claim is integral_V I = integral_V J. Fix zeta as in the statement; K := tsupport zeta is compact, closed and contained in V. Lebesgue measure is translation invariant (integral_add_right_eq_self).
1. Vanishing. zeta(y) = 0 and Dzeta(y) = 0 for y not in K (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), so I(y) = 0 and J(y) = 0 for y not in K (both are linear in Dzeta(y)). As K is contained in V, integral_V I = integral I and integral_V J = integral J over R^n (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero); it suffices to prove integral I = integral J.
2. Points of U. For y in K and t in [0,1], y + (td)e lies in U; in particular y and y + de lie in U. As U is open and u is C^1 on U, Du is continuous at every point of U (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen); g is continuous at every point of U. Psi is C^2, so A is C^1 with derivative B, and A, B are continuous.
3. Continuity principle. If C is a compact subset of R^n and F : R^n -> R vanishes outside C and is continuous at every point of C, then F is continuous (a point outside the closed set C has a neighbourhood on which F = 0) and has compact support (HasCompactSupport.intro), hence is integrable (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport).
4. Integrands. F1(y) := A(Du(y + de))[Dzeta(y)], F2(y) := A(Du(y))[Dzeta(y)] and R2(y) := <zeta(y), g(y)> vanish outside K and are continuous at every point of K (step 2). R3(x) := <zeta(x - de), g(x)> vanishes outside K + de (compact, contained in U by step 2) and is continuous at every point of K + de. By step 3 all four are integrable.
5. Test function zeta. zeta is C^1 with compact support and tsupport zeta = K is contained in U. The hypothesis gives integral_U A(Du(x))[Dzeta(x)] dx = - integral_U <zeta(x), g(x)> dx. Both integrands vanish outside K, a subset of U, so the integrals over U are integrals over R^n: (E2) integral F2 = - integral R2.
6. Translated test function. phi1(x) := zeta(x - de) is C^1 with Dphi1(x) = Dzeta(x - de) (fderiv_comp_sub); it has compact support (composition with the homeomorphism x -> x - de; HasCompactSupport.comp_isClosedEmbedding), and tsupport phi1 = K + de (tsupport_comp_eq_preimage) is contained in U. The hypothesis gives integral_U A(Du(x))[Dzeta(x - de)] dx = - integral_U <zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx. The integrands vanish outside K + de, so these are integrals over R^n; the right one is - integral R3, and translating x = y + de in the left one gives (E1) integral F1 = - integral R3. (Equivalently integral F1 = - integral <zeta(y), g(y + de)> dy, and integral <zeta(y), g(y + de)> dy = integral R3 by translation.)
7. Subtracting (E2) from (E1) and using step 4 (integral_sub): integral (F1 - F2) = integral R2 - integral R3 = integral (R2 - R3) = integral <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx (inner_sub_left).
8. Pointwise FTC. Fix y in K. h(t) := A(P_t(y)) in L* has derivative h'(t) = B(P_t(y))[Delta(y)] (chain rule: t -> P_t(y) is affine with derivative Delta(y)), continuous in t. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt), A(Du(y + de)) - A(Du(y)) = h(1) - h(0) = integral_0^1 B(P_t(y))[Delta(y)] dt, since P_1(y) = Du(y + de) and P_0(y) = Du(y). Evaluating at Dzeta(y) (ContinuousLinearMap.intervalIntegral_apply): F1(y) - F2(y) = integral_0^1 B(P_t(y))[Delta(y)][Dzeta(y)] dt. As Delta(y) = d (d^{-1}Delta(y)) and B(P_t(y)) is linear in its first argument, the integrand equals d B(P_t(y))[d^{-1}Delta(y)][Dzeta(y)], so F1(y) - F2(y) = d I(y). For y not in K both sides vanish (Dzeta(y) = 0). Hence integral (F1 - F2) = d integral I (integral_const_mul).
9. The sibling dohr_eb_elc2_shift_ibp, applied to (U, g, zeta, e, d) (its hypothesis is step 2: x + (td)e in U for x in tsupport zeta and t in [0,1]), gives integral <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx = d integral J.
10. Steps 7, 8 and 9 give d integral I = d integral J. Since d is nonzero, integral I = integral J, and step 1 gives integral_V I = integral_V J. QED
